articles.title: Tajikistan faces growing risks from dependence on labor migration, report warns - Азия-Плюс
articles.summary: Tajikistan faces growing risks from dependence on labor migration, report warns  Азия-Плюс
articles.full_text:
Labor migration helps Tajikistan ease unemployment and support household incomes, but maintaining migration at its current scale could become increasingly difficult in the long term, according to a new report by the Eurasian Fund for Stabilization and Development (EFSD).
The report, titled Economic Growth, Demographics and the Labor Market: Realities and Challenges, was presented on October 29 at the international economic conference Toward Balanced Economic Development in Astana.
According to the report, labor migration remains one of Tajikistan’s main mechanisms for easing pressure on its domestic labor market. With the national economy unable to generate enough jobs for everyone seeking employment, many citizens look for work abroad.
Money sent home by migrant workers helps sustain household consumption, reduce poverty and stimulate domestic demand.
The report notes that remittances have reached the equivalent of nearly half of Tajikistan’s gross domestic product (GDP) in some periods, making it one of the world’s most remittance-dependent economies.
Why does dependence on migration pose risks?
EFSD experts warn that changes in the migration policies of destination countries could make it increasingly difficult for Tajik citizens to find employment abroad.
Russia remains the main destination for Tajik labor migrants. However, tighter migration regulations are limiting the Russian labor market’s ability to absorb foreign workers.
Kazakhstan also attracts workers from neighboring countries, but its labor market remains considerably smaller than Russia’s in terms of employment opportunities for migrants.
Heavy reliance on earnings from abroad also creates challenges for Tajikistan’s domestic economy.
According to the researchers, while remittances boost household spending and imports, they do not necessarily lead to increased domestic production or the creation of more productive, better-paid jobs.
Migration may also discourage some workers from pursuing vocational education and professional training, particularly when jobs available abroad require relatively few qualifications.
Tajikistan’s working-age population to grow by 2.46 million
Demographic trends are expected to put additional pressure on Tajikistan’s labor market over the coming years.
According to EFSD projections, the country’s working-age population, defined as people aged 15–64, will increase from 6.34 million in 2025 to 8.8 million by 2040.
This represents an increase of 2.46 million people over 15 years, potentially creating substantial additional demand for jobs.
EFSD experts argue that Tajikistan cannot rely on labor migration alone to address its employment challenges.
They recommend expanding domestic employment opportunities, supporting private sector development, creating more productive jobs and improving workforce skills.
How dependent is Tajikistan on labor migration?
World Bank data illustrate the scale of Tajikistan’s dependence on money earned abroad.
In 2025, remittances were equivalent to approximately 46% of the country’s GDP, compared with 39% in 2023 and around 49% in 2024.
An estimated one-quarter of Tajikistan’s workforce travels abroad in search of employment.
One of the main drivers of labor migration is the substantial wage gap between Tajikistan and destination countries.
According to the Agency for Statistics under the President of Tajikistan, the average monthly wage in the country stood at 3,508 somoni in July 2026.
The World Bank estimates that Tajik migrants working in Russia can earn at least three times as much as they would in comparable jobs at home, even in relatively low-skilled occupations.
Such dependence leaves Tajikistan vulnerable to developments in Russia’s labor market. Fewer job opportunities, stricter migration regulations or declining migrant earnings could reduce remittance inflows, putting pressure on household incomes and domestic consumption.

Samad Bashirli, Azerbaijan’s Deputy Minister of Economy, participated in the 2nd Tianshan Economic Forum, held in Almaty, Kazakhstan, under the theme “Strengthening Resilient Connectivity and Quality Investments in Central Asia”. The forum was organized by the Central Asia Regional Economic Cooperation (CAREC) Institute.
Addressing a session titled “Investing in Technological Progress, Artificial Intelligence and Digital Connectivity”, held as part of the forum, Bashirli described Central Asia as one of Azerbaijan’s priority areas for partnership.
He highlighted the role of digital transformation in diversifying the economy and enhancing the competitiveness of the non-oil and gas sector. He also briefed participants on measures taken to promote innovation in Azerbaijan and joint projects implemented with countries across the region.
Bashirli underscored the importance of developing partnerships in innovation and artificial intelligence, applying new technologies across various sectors of the economy, and expanding the exchange of knowledge and experience.
The forum explored ways to expand cooperation in trade, energy, transport, logistics and other areas, promote digital trade, advance the application of artificial intelligence and develop human capital.

articles.title: New agreement to help Kremlin track assets of Russians in post-Soviet countries, not including Armenia - CIVILNET
articles.summary: New agreement to help Kremlin track assets of Russians in post-Soviet countries, not including Armenia  CIVILNET
articles.full_text:
By Alexander Pracht
NOTE: The original article erroneously stated that the new regulation would affect Armenia as well as other signatories. However, the original agreement was not signed by Armenia, as per the Russian foreign ministry. We apologize for the confusion.
Russian President Vladimir Putin signed an international agreement Monday with several former Soviet countries, allowing them to exchange banking information to enforce court decisions. The agreement could enable authorities in signatory countries to seek the cross-border seizure of assets based on court rulings.
In addition to Russia, the signatories include Azerbaijan, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.
The agreement, originally signed last year, has faced criticism from civil society groups across the region, who warned that Moscow could use it to obtain information about the financial activities of Russian citizens living abroad.
The agreement will allow Russian authorities to locate debtors’ assets in other countries and subsequently seek their confiscation, lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov told the exiled Russian publication IStories. He also warned that Russian authorities could obtain information about the sources of income of Russians who have left the country for political reasons, potentially exposing them to danger if they are found to have ties to organizations outlawed by Moscow, including media outlets and think tanks critical of the Russian government.
In September, Russia adopted a law allowing authorities to confiscate the assets of people convicted in absentia of activities deemed “extremist” by the Russian state, including, but not limited to, criticism of its invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Do China’s Belt and Road Initiative Investments Generate Spatial Spillovers? Evidence from Nighttime Light Data in Subnational Asia | Global Development Policy Center - Boston University
articles.summary: Do China’s Belt and Road Initiative Investments Generate Spatial Spillovers? Evidence from Nighttime Light Data in Subnational Asia | Global Development Policy Center  Boston University
articles.full_text:
By Yan Wang
Infrastructure plays a central role in economic development. Roads and railways connect producers with markets; power and telecommunications systems support industry, public services and information exchange. However, many developing countries struggle to secure the substantial long-term financing needed for infrastructure.
The Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), launched by China in 2013, seeks to promote infrastructure connectivity, trade and regional economic cooperation. The World Bank predicts that BRI infrastructure investments will increase global real income by 0.7 percent by 2030. By lowering transportation costs and improving access to electricity, these investments are expected to stimulate local economic activity and foster an attractive environment for long-term private investment. Their benefits may also extend beyond project locations as people, goods and capital move more easily across regions.
As of today, more than 140 countries participate in the BRI, with Asia hosting a high concentration of developing economies. The region offers a rich lens to measure BRI’s impact on the local economic development. A new working paper by Xiaolin Wang, Yuan Chang and Yan Wang finds that BRI participation in Asia is associated with a significant increase in local economic activity, and China’s outward infrastructure investment has been a key driver of this effect.
The authors measure regional economic development in Southeast Asia, South Asia and Central Asia using satellite-recorded nighttime light intensity from 2008-2021. They also combine nighttime light data with project-level data from the China’s Overseas Development Finance (CODF) database hosted by the Boston University Global Development Policy Center. The results identify China’s outward infrastructure investment as an important mechanism behind this effect.
The study organizes these infrastructure projects into three categories––point projects (ports, power stations, industrial parks), line projects (roads, railways, oil/gas pipelines) and polygon projects (telecom networks, power-grid coverage areas). Linear projects show particularly strong effects because they can connect markets and lower logistics costs. Across sectors, investments in transportation, power and telecommunications produce stronger economic effects than projects focused on resource extraction.
While certain types of infrastructure yield stronger outcomes, the estimated benefits are most pronounced in countries with closer bilateral ties with China, robust initial economic conditions and lower levels of corruption. Geographically, these impacts prove stronger in areas with greater terrain relief and higher precipitation.
Beyond host countries, evidence points to uneven spatial spillovers across Asia. While these investments generate significant positive spillover effects in South Asia, evidence in Southeast Asia is not robust, and no significant spillovers are observed in Central Asia.
Overall, evidence across Asia confirms that BRI infrastructure investment can support subnational economic development, but its effects depend on infrastructure type and location. To unlock broader regional spillovers, policymakers must prioritize careful project selection, stronger governance and regional coordination.
*

articles.title: Zelenskyy awards Melania Trump top Ukrainian honour after ceasefire helps evacuate nearly 800 people - Geo News
articles.summary: Zelenskyy awards Melania Trump top Ukrainian honour after ceasefire helps evacuate nearly 800 people  Geo News
articles.full_text:
Published November 04, 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has awarded the United States (U.S.) First Lady Melania Trump with the highest Ukrainian state owner, the Order of Princess Olga, for her efforts to secure a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied frontline city of Oleshky.
The presidential decree issued on November 2, 2026, credited Melania with significant personal contribution in humanitarian support of Ukraine. It also acknowledged her leading role in helping the children in the war-torn region.
The Order of Princess Olga, First Class, is conferred upon individuals who have made exceptional contributions in spheres including science, education, culture and charitable work.
Melania, 56, played a key role in negotiating a six-day ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the southern city of Oleshky, allowing humanitarian workers to deliver essential supplies and evacuate residents trapped by the fighting.
The ceasefire, which lasted from October 27 to November 1, marked the longest local pause in fighting since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
According to the First Lady, the humanitarian operation enabled the evacuation of nearly 800 people, including elderly residents and children.
Oleshky, located in the Kherson region, has remained under Russian occupation, with thousands of residents displaced since the war began.
Meanwhile, Melania is scheduled to host representatives from Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday, November 5, to discuss the humanitarian initiative.
Her office said the meeting would focus on the Oleshky ceasefire, with both countries expected to participate

articles.title: What a Democratic Congress can and cannot do about Trump's war, tariffs and visa curbs | HT Explainers - Hindustan Times
articles.summary: What a Democratic Congress can and cannot do about Trump's war, tariffs and visa curbs | HT Explainers  Hindustan Times
articles.full_text:
Democratic control could bring investigations and tougher oversight of Trump’s actions, including the Iran war and sanctions affecting Russian oil.
Democrats will control both chambers of the US Congress from January, with the November 3 midterm elections handing them key victories over the Republicans. That gives the party new powers to investigate, block and withhold money from Donald Trump’s administration, but most of what the President has done abroad since returning to office still rests on authority he can go on using without their votes.
Democratic control will allow the party to pursue investigations into the Iran war, immigration enforcement and allegations of corruption, while blocking Trump's legislation and senior appointments, AFP reported. Robert Garcia, a Democratic congressman from California expected to lead the House Oversight Committee – the chamber's main investigative panel – warned Republicans on social media: “LAWYER UP.”
But, even after January 3, Democrats will lack the 60 Senate votes needed to overcome a filibuster, the tactic that lets a minority block most bills by refusing to end debate, although nominations and some fast-track resolutions need only a simple majority. Trump can also veto any bill passed by the Congress, and overriding it takes two-thirds of both chambers.
James Lindsay of the Council on Foreign Relations, a US think-tank, argues that the party controlling Congress has leverage where a president needs legislative consent, and that Trump has not needed it for the Iran war or his global tariffs as yet.
Iran war: After symbolic vote, fight moves to money
In June, both chambers narrowly passed a resolution directing Trump to halt US military action against Iran, under a 1973 law on when a president may commit US forces to hostilities without the Congress’s approval, Reuters reported. The White House said it was “not constitutional and thus not binding”.
The Iran war, which began on February 28, has cost more than $47 billion, according to Pentagon data reported by Reuters.
A Democratic majority in Congress would add little by voting again, but its real leverage could lie in spending. Democratic lawmakers have introduced measures to ban new funds for the war, though the Pentagon’s existing funds mean operations would not have to stop at once even if the Congress refused new money.
Current government funding expires on December 11, before the new Congress takes office, and Senate Democrats can filibuster a spending bill at the risk of a government shutdown. From January 2027, House Democrats will write the spending bills, and Trump could veto any that bars money for the war.
According to a report published by HT, US forces in West Asia were ready to launch “a big effort” in Iran after the midterms, which – if the plan went ahead – would put fresh operations under way before Democrats can act on funding.
Matt Duss, executive vice-president at the Center for International Policy, a Washington think tank, had told HT he expected hearings on the war and “an attempt to focus on secretary of defense Pete Hegseth, possibly to move forward with an impeachment”. The House can impeach with a simple majority, but removal needs two-thirds of the Senate.
Congress has fewer ways to influence the energy price crisis linked to the war, since the administration has eased supply through executive steps such as the temporary waiver letting countries buy Russian oil.
For India, which wants a swift end to the fighting, the stakes include disrupted shipping, fuel prices and citizen-seafarers killed in attacks on vessels.
The trade war: Tariffs stay with the White House
The administration has held on to its tariffs by moving from one law to another. After the Supreme Court struck down the tariffs Trump had imposed under an emergency-powers law in February, the administration used a trade law that allowed temporary tariffs for up to 150 days, and from July this year, switched to duties under another law, justified by investigations into forced labour. The US Congress handed these powers to presidents decades ago, and taking them back would need a law, which Trump could veto.
The newest tariff power came from the US Congress recently. The Graham Act, which passed with large bipartisan majorities and which Trump signed on September 19, allows tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, with exemptions for European allies but none for India or China.
On October 16, though, Trump waived almost all of its measures, citing the national interest.
India, one of the biggest buyers of Russian oil, had warned Washington that the tariffs could affect bilateral ties. The White House has said it “retains the ability to exercise these authorities at any time”.
Still, Democrats can question these decisions in hearings and refuse any new tariff power Trump seeks. Executive arrangements such as the interim trade framework that India and the US had agreed to in February this year don’t need a Congress vote.
Gregory Meeks, the New York Democrat expected to chair the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has long supported the US-India partnership and has disagreed with the administration's handling of ties with India, HT reported.
Immigration: Congress can weigh in on new large visa fees
Indians accounted for an estimated 71% of approved applications for H-1B visas, which allow US employers to hire skilled foreign workers, in recent years, according to US government figures reported by PTI.
India also sent 363,019 students to the US in 2024-25, more than any other country, according to the Institute of International Education, a US non-profit.
Most of the changes affecting these workers and students came through proclamations and agency rules, which do not need Congress approvals.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) reweighted the H-1B lottery towards higher-paid applicants and ended automatic extensions of work permits for people awaiting renewal. From September 15, students on F-1 visas are admitted for a fixed four-year period instead of for as long as they remain enrolled.
Trump also imposed a $100,000 charge on new H-1B petitions by proclamation in September 2025. In June, Leo Sorokin, a federal judge in Boston, ruled in a case brought by 20 Democratic state attorneys general that “the substance and application of the $100,000 payment reveal that it is a tax”, one that the US Congress never authorised.
Trump renewed the proclamation in September, and the government is appealing the ruling.
DHS has since proposed rebuilding the charge as a fee. A rule published in late August would charge $103,265 for each new H-1B petition subject to the annual cap, under DHS’s power to recover the cost of its services.
The administration is also considering a $100,000 fee on Optional Practical Training (OPT), which lets foreign graduates work in the US after their studies, and a refundable green-card bond of up to $100,000.
If the Boston ruling holds on appeal, charges of this size could need the US Congress’s approval, and a Democratic majority can withhold it. The party would likely do this only if it chooses to fight Trump on legal immigration. So far, Democrats’ fight on immigration this year has been over the use of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.
DHS funding lapsed for 11 weeks from February after Democrats demanded limits on how ICE agents were operating. The deal that ended the shutdown left out ICE and the Border Patrol, which had received more than $130 billion through a budget law last year.
The US Congress has less reach over rules already in force. It can vote to overturn the F-1 rule, but Trump could veto the resolution. And the agency that processes visa petitions is funded mainly by application fees rather than by the Congress, which blunts any attempt to cut off its money.
Also read: Trump's party loses Congress; Democrats seize House, Senate in historic midterm sweep
Ukraine: Where Republicans may break with Trump
Trump’s October 16 order also waived the Graham Act’s sanctions on Russia, and a separate US Treasury licence allows imports of Russian diesel until April 2027.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has said on X that reversing the measures “definitely helps only the Russians”, and lawmakers from both Republicans and Democrats criticised the waiver, Reuters reported.
The Graham Act passed by margins wide enough to override a veto, 86-11 in the Senate and 262-159 in the House, and Russia is the issue on which a bipartisan majority against Trump is most likely to form.
Democrats could try to curb the waiver power by law, but they would need the support of many Republicans to back the Act to vote against the president.
A Ukraine aid bill the House had passed in June over the objections of its Republican leaders stalled in the Senate, AP reported. A Democratic-majority Senate could bring such a bill to a vote, though it would still need 60 votes and Trump’s sign-off.
For India, a Congress pressing harder on Russia would mean closer attention to its purchases of Russian oil, which the waived tariffs targeted.
AI and chips: A narrow bipartisan opening
Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader in the House, who could become its first Black Speaker in January, has said regulating AI will be a legislative priority. Sweeping AI legislation would still need Republican votes in the Senate and could face Trump’s veto.
Lawmakers of both parties have found more common ground on export controls.
After Trump approved sales of Nvidia's H200 AI chips to China, the House Foreign Affairs Committee voted 42-2 in January to advance a bill letting Congress review and block licences to export advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries. A Democratic House would have to revive it in the new Congress, since bills that do not pass before a Congress ends lapse.

articles.title: Uzbekistan plans $300mn airport and infrastructure improvements in Bukhara ahead of international events - Daryo
articles.summary: Uzbekistan plans $300mn airport and infrastructure improvements in Bukhara ahead of international events  Daryo
articles.full_text:
President Shavkat Mirziyoyev held a meeting to review preparations for major international events planned in Bukhara, according to the presidential press service. Discussions focused on transport infrastructure, public safety, urban development and economic cooperation, including plans to construct a new international airport worth $300mn.
During the meeting, Mirziyoyev emphasized that preparations should not be limited to the venues hosting international events. He instructed officials to ensure that the planned improvements cover transport, services, security and urban infrastructure while contributing to the region's development. The president also noted that the events should present Bukhara's historical heritage and current potential.
The meeting reviewed plans to construct a new international airport in Bukhara at a cost of $300mn, alongside the development of a 23.5-kilometer road connecting the airport to the city. The project also includes landscaping along the road.
Mirziyoyev emphasized the importance of improving the condition of airports, railway stations and roads, noting that these facilities are among the first encountered by visitors. Officials were instructed to improve the areas surrounding railway stations, including parking facilities, lighting, passenger services and public transport operations. It was also decided to deploy an additional 120 buses to connect Bukhara city and its districts with railway stations.
The meeting also addressed plans to expand green spaces in Bukhara, taking into account the region's climatic conditions. The proposed measures include planting trees and shrubs and establishing irrigation and drainage systems to ensure their maintenance.
Special attention was given to public safety during the upcoming international events. Plans were discussed to establish modern situation centers in Bukhara, introduce digital monitoring of public spaces and tourist sites, improve traffic management and strengthen measures against cybercrime.
The president also emphasized the need to strengthen cooperation between crime prevention inspectors and the "mahalla seven," a local community governance group, to prevent offenses within neighborhoods.
Mirziyoyev instructed ministries and government agencies to prepare for discussions with foreign partners within their respective areas of responsibility. Officials were tasked with presenting the practical results of reforms implemented in Uzbekistan and developing new joint initiatives.
The meeting reviewed proposals for reaching agreements with foreign partners in industrial cooperation, the production of high value-added goods, transport and logistics, and exports. Discussions also covered the development of renewable energy projects and infrastructure for electricity transmission and storage in the region.
The president emphasized the importance of presenting Bukhara's historical and cultural heritage alongside its tourism and economic potential. Officials were instructed to provide visitors with opportunities to become familiar with the region's modern enterprises, agricultural activities, traditional crafts and service sectors.
The meeting also addressed the need to demonstrate the results of measures aimed at ensuring employment, increasing incomes and developing healthcare and culture. Mirziyoyev instructed officials to present these developments through specific examples.
Mirziyoyev emphasized that facilities constructed and systems introduced during preparations for international events should continue serving Bukhara's residents after the events conclude. Officials were instructed to visit project sites, personally inspect the progress of work, resolve problems on-site and coordinate the implementation of assigned tasks.

articles.title: Russia, Seychelles Bilateral Trade & Relations: October 2026 Update - russia's pivot to asia
articles.summary: Russia, Seychelles Bilateral Trade & Relations: October 2026 Update  russia's pivot to asia
articles.full_text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has met with the Barry Faure, the Seychelles Foreign Minister at the 2026 Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow.
They discussed the development of political, trade, economic, and humanitarian cooperation, as well as international and regional affairs.
Following the discussions, this is what Faure had to say. Our additional comments are prefixed RPA.
Faure: “The Seychelles intends to strengthen ties with Russia not only in tourism and trade, but also in the fight against climate change, ocean protection and the preservation of natural heritage. We intend to diversify our economy, with Russian tourists part of this. Our historical ties continue to influence our bilateral relations.
What we seek in summits like this, is that Seychelles’ national interests are represented in decisions and resolutions which are taken. And I’m happy to say that we see our interests properly reflected.
We have interests in environmental sustainability, biodiversity, ocean governance, climate action, trade, tourism and economic co-operation. We’ve seen all this properly reflected in our bilateral documents, and we are very happy that we have a Seychelles-Russia Action plan for 2027-2029.”
Russia-Africa Climate Resilience
“We’ve also made a very specific proposal that we have been working on since December last year with our Russian counterparts – the creation of a Russian-African mechanism for ensuring climate resilience. It will make it possible to draw on the knowledge and experience of Russia and African countries to combat the negative effects of climate change and, among other things, to mitigate the consequences of natural disasters. So we are happy with this summit.
In April 2026, the President of Seychelles, Dr Patrick Herminie held talks in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin. That was a very important and historic visit. It was the first time that a leader from Seychelles conducted a working visit to Russia. It gave us an opportunity to further advance our relations, which were established 50 years ago and it happened at the time when we were about to celebrate our 50th anniversary of our independence.”
Tourism
“One of our goals was to secure the resumption of Aeroflot flights to the Seychelles before the start of the 2026 summer season. Previously, the airline operated flights there only during certain seasons. And we managed to achieve this. As a result, we saw an increase in the number of Russian tourists. Moreover, despite the consequences of the war in the Middle East, which caused the overall number of tourists visiting the Seychelles to fall, the number of guests from Russia increased. We were also given guarantees that Aeroflot would continue operating flights throughout the year.”
RPA: The tourism industry is currently the focus of bilateral economic ties, with Russian nationals able to enter the Seychelles visa-free for up to 30 days. Russians now account for about 15% of tourist arrivals to the Seychelles, worth an estimated US$180 million in 2025 in revenues to the Seychelles economy. Following the Russia-Africa Summit meetings, Aeroflot have announced that it will increase its flight frequency between Seychelles and Russia to three times a week, operating on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays.
Fisheries
Faure: “Another of our tasks was to ensure the possibility of exporting products from Seychellois fisheries to Russia, since we have substantial fish and other marine resources. This, too, was achieved. In fact, the first consignment of such products will arrive in Russia on Saturday (November 7). The Seychelles will be able to supply its fish products to Russia duty-free.”
RPA: Three Seychellois companies have been approved for supplying fish to Russia by Rosselkhoznadzor, the Russian agency for phytosanitary matters – Ocean Basket, Amirates Fisheries, and Fishtech. The consignment mentioned is fresh tuna, which is being flown directly to Moscow via Aeroflot.
Russian Embassy In The Seychelles
“I should note that we also agreed to open an Embassy of the Seychelles in Russia. I am pleased to announce that, if everything goes according to plan, it will begin operating in the first quarter of 2027.
Our relations with Russia and our bilateral co-operation continue to develop. We have excellent bilateral relations, which have historically been shaped since the times of the Soviet Union. The Soviet Union was one of the first countries to recognise the independence of the Seychelles, and today, Russia continues this line.”
Food Security
“As concerns food security, the priority of our country is to ensure that there is food security and energy supply. We are highly dependent on imports for practically everything: between 90-95% of what we consume is imported. We are therefore highly dependent on global supply chains and international delivery routes.
The war in the Middle East has affected us. We made considerable efforts both internally, using our own means, and externally with our partners, for us to build resilience, for us to build stocks. In fact, we ensured that we have a national system to respond to the impact of the war and to mitigate its repercussions on the population.
The first priority was to make sure that we have essential commodities. We began building up stocks for several months. The same applies to energy supply. We worked with partners to guarantee sufficient fuel supplies. They helped us by providing various goods – from medical supplies to food. We are very grateful to Russia for this assistance.”
Maritime Security
“We have a huge exclusive economic zone. The Seychelles is a small island developing state, the smallest country in Africa, with a population of around 120,000. Our land area is approximately 455 square kilometres. However, the area of our maritime spaces reaches almost 1.4 million square kilometres. So, our small country has to manage a vast area of maritime space.
We provide a platform for international co-operation – both with our closest neighbours and with more distant countries such as Russia, European Union states, the United States and China. We work closely with Mauritius, Madagascar, the Comoros and Réunion. We also interact with India, Sri Lanka, Kenya, Mozambique and other countries. Our task is to ensure the exchange of information and co-ordination of efforts to counter illegal activity at sea.
We not only benefit from such co-operation, but also contribute to the common effort ourselves. In particular, we host the Regional Centre for Operational Co-ordination, which brings together international and regional participants. Information is exchanged at the centre. In addition, we have our own coast guard vessels. Some of them we purchased ourselves, others we received as gifts from friendly countries, including India and China. We make these resources available to the entire region, because helping the region also helps us. Support from the international community also serves our interests.
Various types of illicit maritime activities take place in our maritime spaces. These include illegal fishing, as well as drug trafficking across vast ocean spaces. We also face human trafficking. Smuggling also occurs, including on islands belonging to us that have no permanent population but possess significant natural resources. All of this creates security threats.
It is therefore extremely important for us to exercise sovereign control over our maritime spaces. We can achieve this only through co-operation with our closest neighbours, regional partners and countries beyond our region.”
RPA: It should be noted that the Russian Navy’s Pacific Fleet frigate Marshal Shaposhnikov has docked at the port of Victoria in the Seychelles. The Pacific Fleet frigate Marshal Shaposhnikov arrived at Victoria Port in the Seychelles on November 2. Russian sailors were welcomed at the port by representatives of the Russian Embassy and the Seychelles Navy command. During the ship’s stay in the Seychelles, joint Russian-Seychelles naval anti-piracy drills will be held for the first time.
Education
Faure: “Our educational ties are also important. Russia was one of the first countries that came to Seychelles with programmes of collaboration in education, vocational training, and cultural and sports exchanges. More than 100 students from the Seychelles have studied at various Russian universities.
Our country’s Vice-President, Vincent Meriton, who held that post in 2016–2020, received his education in Moscow in sociology. He still plays a very important role in the life of the Seychelles today, since he heads the Seychelles-Russia Friendship Society.
There have been other similar examples. One of our country’s leading theatre directors trained at the Bolshoi Theatre. He plays an important role in developing the culture of the Seychelles, working on films and on the development of young Seychellois cinema.”
RPA: The director mentioned is John Poole Etienne, who has also been involved in organising the first ballet events in the Seychelles, introducing the local population to Tchaikovsky and other Russian cultural figures.
Faure: “All of this contributes to shaping national identity and developing our country’s culture, as well as strengthening relations, friendship and contacts between our peoples. All of this has also influenced the decisions we take as a state.”
RPA: Russia and the Seychelles maintain educational cooperation. Seychellois nationals can study in Russian universities based on a government-funded scholarship program. Russia also helps retrain Seychellois police officers and intelligence agents, while the Seychelles government has recently begun Russian language training classes for employees in the tourism sector.

articles.summary: Russia, Burundi Bilateral Trade & Relations: October 2026 Update  russia's pivot to asia
articles.full_text:
The Russian President, Vladimir Putin met with the President of Burundi, Evariste Ndayishimiye, on the sidelines of the 2026 Russia–Africa Summit in Moscow.
Taking part in the meeting on the Russian side were Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak, Deputy Chief of Staff of the Presidential Executive Office Maxim Oreshkin, Deputy Chief of Staff of the Presidential Executive Office – Presidential Press Secretary Dmitry Peskov, Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov, Russian Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Burundi Sergei Chernenko, Minister of Economic Development Maxim Reshetnikov, and Head of the Federal Service for the Oversight of Consumer Protection and Welfare Anna Popova, Deputy Foreign Minister Georgy Borisenko, Deputy Defence Minister Vasily Osmakov, and Director General of the State Space Corporation Roscosmos Dmitry Bakanov.
Ndayishimiye is the current Chair of the African Union and spent a considerable amount of time with Putin as part of this role. We covered their joint press conference regarding the 2026 Russia-Africa Summit here. However, bilateral ties are also increasing. In this article we examine their mutual trade and investment relations. This is what they had to say on the subject:
Vladimir Putin: “I would like to thank you for your substantial contribution to the success of our summit. We are developing relations with the African Union, which you currently chair, on a solid, long-term basis. As you know, we supported the African Union’s aspiration to become a full member of the G20.
Our bilateral relations are developing well, and our ties continue to grow stronger. We can discuss what further steps might be taken to ensure that our economic cooperation, alongside our political engagement, helps advance our shared plans for strengthening these long-standing bilateral ties. Next year, we will mark the 65th anniversary of diplomatic relations between our countries.
I am also aware that a ceremony was held yesterday to confer upon you the title of Honorary Doctor of the Patrice Lumumba Peoples’ Friendship University of Russia. Please accept my warmest congratulations on this occasion.”
Ndayishimiye: “Thank you very much, dear friend, for this opportunity. This meeting has confirmed that Russia wants to move forward together with Africa. As I have said, you have stood with us since the beginning of our struggle for decolonisation, supporting us in our quest for independence. Today we are in a different era – an era of development, and we are very grateful to Russia for its support.
Thank you for supporting us in this new phase – the phase of liberation, the pursuit for economic autonomy for African countries. All African countries understand that we have opportunities, but we lack the capital to get everything started. Because we need a solid framework for this.
What is that framework? It is an international plan. We would like to thank Russia once again for supporting our bid to become a full member of the UN Security Council and our aspiration to join the G20. We will continue in this spirit, hoping that Africa will achieve a strong position on the international stage, enabling us to advance our social and economic spheres.
Burundi has opportunities, we have natural resources and capital, we have a very dynamic young population and, in principle, we have the finances. What we lack is finance and technology to create basic infrastructure – in transport, in energy, in digital systems. We do not have all this at present. But I believe that together we can move forward. Russia has such capital, and we hope that at this new stage, we will be able to cooperate and to see how we can invest more and build a mutually beneficial partnership.
We have a great wealth of natural resources, and we need capital to process them and create value chains. The last time we met, I told you about our projects – socioeconomic projects in particular. Yes, we faced some difficulties: at that time the West imposed sanctions against us – there was Western interference. We continue to suffer from this.
We have budgetary problems and we cannot, receive funding from the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund. That is why I asked for assistance with chemical fertilisers, and I would like to repeat that request once again.
We have also asked for help in protecting our institutions. We are in close proximity to the Democratic Republic of the Congo and you know that there is a conflict underway in its eastern regions.”
Burundi is a landlocked, resource-poor country with an underdeveloped manufacturing sector. The economy is predominantly agricultural, accounting for about 50% of GDP, while employing more than 90% of the population. Subsistence agriculture accounts for 90% of agriculture. Burundi’s primary exports are coffee and tea, which account for 90% of foreign exchange earnings, though exports are a relatively small share of GDP. Other agricultural products include cotton, tea, maize, sorghum, sweet potatoes, bananas, manioc (tapioca), beef, milk and cow hides.
Burundi is one of the world’s poorest nations, owing in part to its landlocked geography, a lack of education and the proliferation of HIV/AIDS. Famines and food shortages have occurred throughout Burundi, and according to the World Food Programme, 56.8% of children under age five suffer from chronic malnutrition. Burundi’s export earnings – and its ability to pay for imports – rests primarily on weather conditions and international coffee and tea prices. Apart from agriculture, other industries include the assembly of imported components; public works construction; food processing; and light consumer goods such as blankets, shoes, and soap.
Burundi does have some natural resources; however, investment will be needed to extract these. They include uranium, nickel, cobalt, copper and platinum.
Burundi joined the East African Community (EAC) in 2009 and is also a member of the African Continental Free Trade Agreement.
With a mainly Christian population of just over 14 million and covering an area of 27,834 km², Burundi’s GDP (PPP) is estimated at US$14 billion, with a GDP per capita (PPP) of just US$1,020. It has a low Human Development Index, although there is some sign of progress – 2026 GDP growth is estimated to reach 4.7%.
Russia, Burundi Bilateral Trade & Investment
Burundi and Russia have a small, but growing trade relationship that includes services, and cooperation in industry, mining, and agriculture. Russia exports wheat, potassic fertilizers, iron, steel and vehicles to Burundi; with bulgar wheat in particular used in traditional Burundian dishes such as Boko Boko Harees.
Burundi exports small amounts of coffee to Russia. Current bilateral trade however is small at about US$10 million.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov announced in 2024 that an inter-governmental agreement on nuclear energy was being discussed. In addition, the two sides have discussed hydropower projects, saying that Russian companies were prepared to invest in the country. If these materialise, they will probably be financed at least in part-exchange from Burundi’s mineral assets.
Burundi is keen on constructing small modular nuclear power stations, with Lavrov saying in July this year that during a visit to Burundi that “We discussed a whole host of specific projects that Russian companies are ready to implement in Burundi, primarily in the hydropower and nuclear power sectors.” On nuclear power, work is already underway; staff are being trained. Burundi is keen on small modular nuclear power stations, and Rosatom and Burundi’s counterparts have already signed a fundamental document that forms the basis for such interaction.” That appears feasible, as Burundi has significant uranium and nickel reserves.
Education is another cooperation sector, with Lavrov adding that “Our African colleagues are increasingly interested in educational exchanges. We are ready, at our friends’ request, to increase the number of annual stipends allocated to Burundi.”
Russia also resumed flour exports to Burundi this year after a hiatus beginning in November 2024. Over 815 tonnes of wheat or rye-wheat flour worth around US$600,000 were shipped in 8M 2026, according to the Russian Agroexport Federal Center.
There may additionally be manufacturing opportunities, depending upon regional overland supply chains to neighbouring countries, to develop Burundi as a light industrial assembly hub for export to EAS members due to the lower wages and its central-eastern location.

articles.title: Pakistan BRICS Membership Could Strengthen Its Strategic Ties with China - The Daily CPEC
articles.summary: Pakistan BRICS Membership Could Strengthen Its Strategic Ties with China  The Daily CPEC
articles.full_text:
BRICS, China and Pakistan: A New Diplomatic Opportunity
Pakistan BRICS membership could offer Islamabad an opportunity to strengthen its position in a changing global order. Beyond joining a larger economic bloc, closer engagement with BRICS could help Pakistan deepen its strategic partnership with China and build stronger economic and diplomatic ties with other emerging economies.
For Pakistan, this ambition is closely connected with its long-standing strategic partnership with China. As BRICS expands its economic and diplomatic role, greater engagement with the grouping could give Pakistan another platform to strengthen cooperation with Beijing while developing ties with other major emerging economies.
Pakistan formally applied for BRICS membership in November 2023, presenting its interest as part of its commitment to inclusive multilateralism and international cooperation. The application remains an important part of Islamabad’s wider diplomatic strategy. However, membership is not guaranteed, and Pakistan must continue building support among existing members.
Pakistan BRICS Membership and China’s Strategic Role
China remains central to Pakistan’s approach to BRICS. In 2026, the two countries marked 75 years of diplomatic relations, commemorating a partnership that has developed across political, economic and security cooperation.
During Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s official visit to China from 23 to 26 May 2026, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to deepening the China-Pakistan All-Weather Strategic Cooperative Partnership. Their joint statement of 26 May 2026 outlined cooperation across trade, investment, agriculture, energy, technology, artificial intelligence and regional connectivity.
The China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) remains one of the most visible expressions of this relationship. Its first phase supported major investments in energy and infrastructure. According to Pakistan’s CPEC Secretariat, Phase I attracted approximately US$25 billion in Chinese investment and added nearly 8,000 MW to Pakistan’s power-generation capacity.
The next phase, CPEC 2.0, is expected to place greater emphasis on industrial development, agriculture, minerals, technology, human-resource development and business-to-business cooperation. This broader economic agenda gives Pakistan a stronger foundation for engaging with China on issues that also feature prominently in BRICS discussions.
How BRICS Membership Could Expand Pakistan’s Economic Opportunities
BRICS has changed considerably since its formation by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.
The grouping now comprises 11 members: Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the United Arab Emirates. Its expansion has increased its representation across the Global South and broadened the scope of its economic and diplomatic cooperation. The Indian government’s overview of BRICS provides the current membership details.
The 18th BRICS Summit, held in New Delhi on 12–13 September 2026, placed emphasis on resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. The adopted New Delhi Declaration reaffirmed the group’s commitment to reforming global governance and strengthening economic cooperation.
Its priorities included cross-border payment mechanisms, trade settlements in local currencies, artificial intelligence, financial technology, digital security and sustainable development. These areas reflect a broader effort to strengthen practical cooperation among member economies rather than limiting BRICS to political dialogue.
Pakistan BRICS membership remains an important part of Islamabad’s efforts to strengthen its engagement with emerging economies. Although the country is not yet a member, the expanded grouping offers a platform for exploring wider economic and diplomatic cooperation.
CPEC 2.0 and Pakistan’s Wider BRICS Opportunities
Pakistan does not need to view BRICS and CPEC as separate diplomatic or economic tracks. CPEC provides an established foundation for Pakistan-China cooperation, while greater engagement with BRICS could create opportunities to connect that relationship with additional markets, institutions and development partners.
For Pakistan BRICS membership could also create opportunities to connect CPEC-related economic cooperation with wider markets and investment networks. However, these benefits would depend on practical agreements and stronger commercial partnerships.
CPEC 2.0 is particularly relevant to this approach. In their May 2026 joint statement, Pakistan and China agreed to advance the high-quality development of the upgraded CPEC framework. They identified industrial parks, agriculture, mining, digital economy, artificial intelligence, scientific innovation and trade cooperation as areas for deeper engagement.
The emphasis is also shifting towards private-sector participation and commercially driven projects. This transition is important because long-term economic gains will depend not only on infrastructure but also on productive industries, stronger exports and investment that generates employment.
Pakistan’s broader economic cooperation with China is already moving in this direction. The Daily CPEC’s analysis, Ahsan Urges Private Sector to Drive CPEC 2.0, examines the growing emphasis on industrial development, business partnerships and private-sector investment.
If Pakistan eventually joins BRICS, its existing relationship with China could provide a useful starting point for participating in cooperation on industrial development, technology, infrastructure and regional connectivity. However, membership alone would not automatically produce investment or trade opportunities. Pakistan would still need to develop competitive industries and create conditions that attract long-term business partnerships.
Pakistan’s Diplomatic Approach
Pakistan’s BRICS application also reflects a broader approach to international diplomacy. Islamabad maintains important relationships with China, the Gulf states, Central Asian countries, Russia and Western institutions. Greater engagement with one partner does not necessarily require reducing cooperation with another.
BRICS could add another dimension to this approach. Multilateral platforms allow countries to pursue shared economic interests while maintaining their individual bilateral relationships. For Pakistan, the opportunity lies in using these platforms to expand diplomatic engagement and develop practical economic connections.
The May 2026 Pakistan-China joint statement also reflected this wider outlook. Both countries expressed support for an inclusive global economic order and an equal and orderly multipolar international system. They also agreed to strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence and support international collaboration on its governance.
These priorities are relevant to Pakistan’s ambition to participate more actively in discussions about emerging technologies and the future of the global economy. Cooperation with China could help strengthen its capacity in these areas, while wider BRICS engagement could provide additional opportunities for dialogue and knowledge-sharing.
Pakistan’s BRICS Bid and the India Factor
Pakistan BRICS membership prospects are shaped by a complicated regional environment. India is a founding BRICS member and hosted the 2026 summit in New Delhi, making regional diplomacy an important consideration in Islamabad’s application.
BRICS decisions on membership require consensus among existing members. This means Pakistan’s application cannot be considered separately from its diplomatic relations with the countries already in the grouping.
India’s position therefore remains an important factor in Pakistan’s membership prospects. Islamabad will need to pursue a diplomatic approach that emphasises economic cooperation, regional stability and inclusive multilateralism rather than allowing the application to become another extension of regional rivalry.
Nevertheless, Pakistan can continue developing relationships with BRICS members regardless of the outcome of its application. Bilateral trade, investment discussions and diplomatic engagement do not depend entirely on full membership.
The immediate objective should therefore extend beyond securing a place in the grouping. Building stronger connections with its members can offer practical benefits even before any membership decision is reached.
A Chance to Build New Economic Connections
Greater engagement with BRICS could help Pakistan explore new opportunities in agriculture, minerals, technology, pharmaceuticals, engineering, manufacturing and digital services.
These sectors also feature in Pakistan’s evolving economic cooperation with China. The Daily CPEC’s report, Pakistan-China Digital Corridor: Tech and CPEC 2.0, examines how technology exports, professional services and cross-border business partnerships could complement traditional infrastructure cooperation.
Infrastructure and regional connectivity offer another opportunity. Pakistan’s geographical position gives it potential to connect South Asia with China, Central Asia and the Middle East. CPEC and the development of Gwadar Port provide an important foundation for these ambitions.
Stronger engagement with BRICS economies could help Pakistan explore additional trade and investment links around that foundation. However, the country would need competitive exports, reliable infrastructure, stronger industrial capacity and a business environment capable of attracting long-term investors.
China as a Strategic Advantage
Pakistan’s relationship with China gives it an established starting point for deeper engagement with emerging economies. The two countries are already working to move CPEC beyond its original infrastructure focus towards a broader partnership involving industry, technology, agriculture, innovation and human-resource development.

articles.title: Beijing’s Belt and Road Is Failing the Hormuz Stress Test — And Canada Still Has $1 Billion Committed to Xi’s Infrastructure Bank - The Bureau | Sam Cooper
articles.summary: Beijing’s Belt and Road Is Failing the Hormuz Stress Test — And Canada Still Has $1 Billion Committed to Xi’s Infrastructure Bank  The Bureau | Sam Cooper
articles.full_text:
By Mehmet Tohti
OTTAWA — For more than a decade, Beijing has sold the Belt and Road Initiative as the destiny of humanity — a vision of common connectivity and prosperity. Ports, railways and pipelines would bind Asia, Africa and Europe to China through several land corridors, the “Belt,” while the Maritime Silk Road, the “Road,” would carry Chinese goods outward and Gulf energy inward. Beijing even declared China a “near-Arctic state” to fold a Polar Silk Road into the design. Geography, finance and ambition would do the rest.
Since February 28, when the United States and Israel launched their air war on Iran, the world’s most important energy chokepoint, the Strait of Hormuz, has been largely shut. In early October, the International Monetary Fund’s PortWatch counted just four transits in a single day, compared with a pre-war norm of 85. Ships are being struck almost daily. The International Energy Agency calls it the largest energy security crisis the world has ever faced.
This is the stress test the Belt and Road was never designed to pass, and it is failing dramatically.
The failure reaches into Canada, too.
Ottawa still has close to US$1 billion committed to Beijing’s Belt and Road-style infrastructure bank, despite freezing its participation in 2023 after a Canadian insider, Bob Pickard, walked out and went public with allegations of covert Chinese Communist Party control over the multilateral lender, which is backed in part by Western taxpayers.
Roughly 40 percent of China’s crude imports came from the six Persian Gulf states in 2025. By June 2026, China’s imports had fallen to a decade low of 7.12 million barrels a day, down 41 percent from a year earlier. Russian supplies to China increased, and the initial shock was absorbed.
But absorbing a shock is not the same as commanding a trade route. The Maritime Silk Road’s most important leg now operates with the permission of Iran’s Revolutionary Guard. The Guard set up a “toll booth” off Larak Island, charging around $2 million per supertanker, payable in Chinese yuan. Chinese ships were waved through as “friendly” vessels, sometimes without paying the toll, with their passage timed to suit Tehran’s diplomacy. Others were turned back. The White House said Xi Jinping opposed the tolls at his May summit with President Trump, even as Chinese tankers kept passing with Iran’s blessing.
Meanwhile, much of the traffic that does move is protected by the United States Navy. China’s maritime road depends on the goodwill of a revolutionary militia and the protection of its chief strategic rival.
Beijing foresaw the vulnerability of maritime chokepoints and sought to answer it with a land alternative. Rail corridors from Korla in East Turkistan were meant to reach Iran, Türkiye and Europe, bypassing the reach of any navy. That was the plan.
The war has cut into that hedge too. Rail and road links running from Iran toward Türkiye and Central Asia have been disrupted or severed. In the Red Sea, Houthi attacks around the Bab el-Mandeb once again threaten the Suez route to Europe. The southern land corridor and the sea lane are failing at the same time.
The flagship new line, from Kashgar through Kyrgyzstan to Andijan in Uzbekistan, is still a construction site. It is expected to reach just 22 percent of planned work by the end of 2026, with a target opening of 2030. Today, China’s trains to Europe still cross Kazakhstan, then Russia or the Caspian.
And rail carries containers, not oceans of crude. No railway can replace the millions of barrels a day that tankers once brought from the Gulf.
If any initiative was meant to prove its value during this crisis, it was the Gwadar project. The $62 billion China–Pakistan Economic Corridor links Kashgar by road to a deep-water port about 600 kilometers east of Hormuz. On paper, it is the bypass Beijing always wanted.
In practice, Gwadar has become a temporary buffer, not a trade hub. Its port chairman celebrated receiving six diverted transshipment cargoes during the crisis, the first in more than a decade — a rounding error for a global gateway. Saudi and Kuwaiti discussions about storing oil there remain preliminary. A Pakistani port official identified the obstacle plainly: security.
A crisis that should have proved the corridor’s worth has instead exposed how little of it was ever built.
Worse for Beijing, its oldest partner — the country that once described its relations with China as deeper than ocean, sweeter than honey and stronger than steel — is hedging.
Since 2025, Pakistan has rebuilt its ties with Washington. Its army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, lunched with President Trump at the White House in June 2025 and returned with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif in September. Islamabad offered American access to its critical minerals and signed a $500 million rare earths deal with a US firm.
Then came the boldest move. Munir’s advisers proposed that the United States build and run a port at Pasni, about 110 kilometers east of Gwadar. The pitch reportedly cited “dual-use concerns” about Chinese ports. It envisioned some $1.2 billion in investment and a rail link to Balochistan’s mineral belt. Islamabad has not adopted it as official policy, and Washington has not said whether it accepts.
The country Beijing called its “iron brother” is offering its rival a harbor beside China’s flagship port. Gwadar was meant to anchor the Maritime Silk Road in a loyal client state. It now sits on a coast where Washington is welcome too.
Beijing assumed Central Asia was its uncontested hinterland. That assumption is also unraveling.
On October 17, Chinese Premier Li Qiang was in Tashkent, where Uzbekistan’s presidency put the portfolio of Chinese-backed projects at nearly $60 billion. The next day, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio landed in Samarkand, the ancient Silk Road city, for a C5+1 meeting with all five Central Asian foreign ministers. He brought more than 200 American business leaders with him.
The momentum began at the C5+1 leaders’ summit hosted in Washington on November 6, 2025. Around that summit, Uzbekistan pledged to buy and invest nearly $35 billion in American sectors over three years. Uzbek-American trade grew by a third in the first eight months of 2026.
The numbers still favor Beijing. But the message to Central Asian capitals is clear: they have alternatives for their long-term stability and security. The Kashgar–Andijan railway — Beijing’s principal overland route bypassing Russian transit — terminates in Uzbekistan, a nation increasingly courted by Washington. With these developments, China’s land routes no longer cross a secure sphere of influence, but rather contested ground once considered its backyard.
Washington should use that leverage for more than contracts. Central Asian governments have faced Chinese pressure to align their positions with Beijing’s on the Uyghur genocide, transnational repression and other issues. Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan have all, at various times, sent back Uyghurs who had fled persecution.
The Uyghur region shares international borders with eight nations — Mongolia, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Afghanistan, Pakistan and India — making it China’s primary land bridge to Central Asia, South Asia and the broader Eurasian landmass. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan Railway (Kashgar–Andijan), the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor to Gwadar, northern rail links through Khorgos and Alashankou into Kazakhstan, and Central Asian natural gas pipelines all converge on or originate within the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, which its original inhabitants call East Turkistan.
As the sea becomes less reliable, the land becomes more precious to Beijing. That makes the region more central to China’s economic security, and its people more exposed. A regime that already treats Uyghur identity as a security threat will not loosen its grip on its most important transit corridor. The wave of decrees and legislation Beijing has issued over the past six months tightens that grip further, signaling the government’s acute sense of vulnerability there.
The world should understand what “connectivity” means on the ground from the experience of Uyghurs. The road west is being paved through a region of genocide, mass surveillance, internment, transnational repression and forced labor.
Three Years After Freezing Ties, Canada’s Capital Remains in Beijing’s Infrastructure Bank
Beijing built financial institutions to match its corridors. The flagship is the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), launched in 2016 as Xi Jinping’s answer to the World Bank and the IMF.
In March 2018, Canada became the bank’s first North American member, committing to a total share subscription of US$995.4 million, which includes US$199.1 million in paid-in capital. The promise was lucrative contracts for Canadian firms, but few ever materialized.
In June 2023, the bank’s Canadian communications chief, Bob Pickard, resigned. He alleged that the bank was dominated by Communist Party members and served Beijing’s agenda. Ottawa froze all government-led activity and ordered a review. That December, it expanded the review and suspended Canada’s participation indefinitely.
In interviews with The Bureau, Pickard has argued that while the AIIB is not officially called a Belt and Road bank by Beijing, it operates within the Chinese Communist Party’s plans to boost the Belt and Road system.
More than three years later, Global Affairs Canada officials told members of Parliament in late October that they could not say whether the review had concluded. Canada’s capital still sits on the bank’s books in Beijing.
This limbo is the worst of both worlds.
Canada’s money remains tied up, while Canada has no meaningful voice in how it is used. Moody’s, which rates the bank, has noted that Canada holds only about 1 percent of its shares. Beijing does not need our capital. It values our name on its membership list.
T

articles.title: Political earthquake in Washington, what awaits Ukraine, Iran, Israel and Azerbaijan? - Modern.az
articles.summary: Political earthquake in Washington, what awaits Ukraine, Iran, Israel and Azerbaijan?  Modern.az
articles.full_text:
The Democrats' takeover of both houses of Congress in America does not only change the internal political landscape of the United States. This result has the power to affect a number of geopolitical processes, from the war in Ukraine to the Middle East, from relations with Russia to competition with China, from the South Caucasus to the global economy. The eyes of the world are once again on Washington.
The result from the ballot boxes in America is actually a bigger event than one political party winning over another. This is a change in the balance of political power in the second phase of Donald Trump's rule, a narrowing of the White House's room for maneuver, and the emergence of the possibility of a new institutional confrontation in US foreign policy.
In the November 3, 2026 midterm elections, Democrats gained a majority in both the Senate and the House of Representatives. This result is considered as a voter reaction to Trump's political course. In particular, economic difficulties, rising prices, the war with Iran and the administration's foreign policy decisions are among the main factors affecting the election results.
The US political system has its own unique characteristics. The president heads the executive branch of the country, while Congress holds the mechanisms of legislation, budget, approval of appointments, and control over the executive branch.
Now the possibility of these two centers of power operating with different political wills is increasing.
Democrats will control both houses of Congress starting January 3. Of course, the current situation will create a serious obstacle to Trump's legislative initiatives. It seems that Trump's appointments will also become more difficult.
However, we must also emphasize that Trump has not yet lost his presidency. His veto power, executive orders, and authority to make diplomatic decisions remain. This means that a change in the balance of power within the government is taking place in America. To be more specific, Washington is entering a new phase of institutional confrontation.
_n
The struggle between Republicans and Democrats in America is a struggle over which line the country's domestic and foreign policy will be built on.
Republicans, especially Trump's political line, are built on national sovereignty, protectionism, strict migration policy, tariff mechanisms, and bilateral deals. Trump prefers direct political and economic agreements in international relations, rather than the traditional alliance system.
Democrats, on the other hand, traditionally prioritize multilateral diplomacy, cooperation with NATO and other international institutions, coordination with allies, and the preservation of a liberal international order.
This difference should not be absolutized either. Democrats also take a tough stance in strategic competition with China. Among Republicans, there are forces that advocate support for Ukraine and want to increase pressure on Russia. The main difference is not so much in the goals, but in the means chosen to achieve those goals.
Trump's policy relies more on individual leadership, political pressure, and economic levers. The Democrats' approach is closer to institutional coordination and collective decision-making with allies.
The victory of the Democrats is also a serious message to Trump's political influence. The voter actually evaluated the administration's activities. This result may also affect the political configuration of the 2028 presidential elections. But it is wrong to think that Trump has withdrawn from the political scene. On the contrary, the new resistance in Congress may also cause the White House to choose a tougher political tactic.
Russia-Ukraine war, will Washington's account with Moscow change?
One of the most interesting issues in the world is this: How will the Democrats' majority in Congress affect the fate of the Ukrainian war? The answer to this question interests Moscow, Kyiv, and Europe.
During the Trump administration, serious changes occurred in Washington's attitude towards Ukraine. The previous administration's large-scale military and financial support model weakened, and issues of reviewing negotiations and sanctions policy in relations with Russia came to the fore.
Democrats, on the other hand, criticize Trump's relations with Moscow and the reduction of support for Ukraine.
Now the new political balance in Congress can create additional opportunities for Ukraine.
It can be assumed that Democrats will put forward legislative initiatives to increase military and financial aid to Ukraine. The issue of tightening sanctions mechanisms against Russia will be on the agenda again. Possible agreements between the White House and Moscow will face more serious political and institutional control in Congress. The coordination opportunities of European countries with Washington on the issue of supporting Ukraine will increase.
Moscow, on the other hand, will face another problem. In parallel with the diplomatic relations it established with the Trump administration, Russia will have to reckon with tougher positions in Congress.
Thus, in Washington's relations with Moscow, a dual political center will emerge, with Trump in the White House and a new political force dominated by Democrats in Congress. All this means a more complex diplomatic environment for the Kremlin than before.
How will the Iran-Israel confrontation be...
One of the most serious geopolitical consequences of the elections in America will be felt in the Middle East. Because in any case, the US and Israel's war with Iran will go beyond the regional security plane and directly affect energy markets, international trade, oil prices, maritime transport, and global economic stability.
The economic burden created by the war has also entered the daily lives of American voters. Rising prices, energy costs, and the financing of military operations have become one of the factors weakening the Trump administration's political positions.
The new Democratic Congress may bring the issue of financing this war and the president's military powers to a more serious discussion. The main issue here is the constitutional control of war powers.
The US Congress can limit additional funding for military operations, investigate the administration's decisions, and exert political pressure on the legal basis of the war.
New discussions may also arise on the issue of military aid to Israel. In particular, issues of civilian safety, arms export control, and the compliance of military operations with international law will occupy a more prominent place on the Democrats' agenda.
However, support for Israel is not only the position of Republicans in US politics. There is also a strong political group among Democrats who consider Israel's security a strategic interest.
Therefore, it is not about Washington turning its back on Israel. It is about the possibility of changing the conditions of support, political control, and the future model of military cooperation.
For Iran, the election results may also create certain diplomatic opportunities. Of course, Tehran will seek a new platform for negotiations by taking advantage of the strengthening of political resistance to the war within the US.
But let's not forget that the victory of the Democrats does not automatically mean the normalization of relations with Iran. Iran's nuclear program, regional military activities, and security issues will remain on Washington's political agenda.
The biggest risk is the transition period until January. The possibility of the Trump administration escalating militarily before the new Congress begins its work will further complicate the regional situation.
China, the common rival of two parties
There is a direction in American foreign policy where there is a serious strategic closeness between Democrats and Republicans. This is competition with China. Although the election results in Washington may create certain tactical changes for Beijing, it would not be correct to expect the strategic competition to stop.
Trump uses tariffs, trade restrictions, and economic pressure mechanisms against China. Democrats, on the other hand, pay special attention to technological superiority, the semiconductor industry, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and international partnerships in competition with China. That is, although the tools of struggle are different, the main strategic goal is similar, protecting the US's global economic and technological superiority is a priority. The new Congress will more seriously investigate Trump's tariff policy and trade relations with China. All this does not guarantee a softening of relations with Beijing.
The main issue for China is to correctly assess the opportunities arising from the political fragmentation of the US. Beijing may try to expand its economic partnerships in Asia, Africa, Europe, and the Middle East in this situation. In short, the political balance in Washington is changing, but the US-China strategic competition continues.
South Caucasus, what should Baku, Yerevan and Tbilisi expect?
The impact of political changes in America on our region also requires special attention.
The South Caucasus is currently one of the places where the geopolitical interests of great powers intersect. The foreign policy choices of Azerbaijan, Armenia, and Georgia, regional transport corridors, energy security, and relations with Russia are the main directions of this competition. Economic interests, energy routes, and strategic transit opportunities play an important role in the Trump administration's approach to the region.

articles.title: Uzbekistan and Germany discuss increasing bilateral trade to $2bn - Daryo
articles.summary: Uzbekistan and Germany discuss increasing bilateral trade to $2bn  Daryo
articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan and Germany have discussed increasing bilateral trade turnover from $1.4bn to $2bn during a meeting at Uzbekistan's Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade with German Ambassador Matthias Follert. The meeting focused on strengthening trade, economic and investment cooperation, expanding industrial collaboration and implementing joint projects between the two countries.
During the meeting, the parties discussed further strengthening trade, economic and investment cooperation between Uzbekistan and Germany. Particular attention was paid to increasing bilateral trade turnover from $1.4bn to $2bn and developing cooperation with leading German companies.
Currently, 253 enterprises with German capital participation operate in Uzbekistan. The meeting also addressed expanding industrial collaboration and implementing joint projects between Uzbekistan and Germany. The parties discussed developing cooperation with leading German companies.
The parties reviewed preparations for an upcoming visit to Uzbekistan by a delegation from the Eastern Committee of the German Economy. They also discussed preparations for the 18th meeting of the Intergovernmental Working Group on Trade and Investment, scheduled to take place in Berlin. Following the meeting, both sides reaffirmed their mutual interest in further deepening practical cooperation and strengthening business ties between Uzbekistan and Germany.
Earlier Daryo reported that Timur Mashanpin, Deputy Director of Uzbekistan's Agency for Technical Regulation, held talks with Nadine Tatge, coordinator of Germany's "Support for Reforms in the National Quality Infrastructure" project, on strengthening bilateral cooperation in technical regulation. The parties acknowledged the positive results of intergovernmental negotiations on financial and technical cooperation between Uzbekistan and Germany for 2026–2027.
The meeting covered cooperation in standardization, metrology and conformity assessment, alongside specialist training and closer engagement with Uzbekistan's industrial enterprises. The participants also discussed aligning national legislation and technical regulations with World Trade Organization (WTO) requirements.
